problem: Forty years of performance research have produced sophisticated diagnostic tools, but most of them stop at identifying the problem. A Roofline plot, a stall report, or a list of hardware counters tells a developer where a GPU kernel is slow, not what code to change. Turning that diagnosis into an edit still takes architectural expertise that few developers have.
importance: Without actionable guidance, the skill gap widens: only a small group of experts can write or optimize efficient scientific code, and everyone else is left with large volumes of diagnostic data and no clear next step. Large language models write code, but on their own they do not close this gap. When we gave an LLM only the GPU source code, it produced no optimization that improved performance.
challenges: Prior LLM work on code optimization relies on static analysis or prompt tuning, so it never sees stalls, occupancy, or memory throughput, the signals that decide real performance. Adding those signals is not a matter of pasting a profile into a prompt: raw PC-sampling output for a single 41-line kernel is 990 MB, far beyond any model's context window. The diagnostic sources can also point to different causes, and an LLM can write edits that compile but miss the actual bottleneck.
approach:
We first built Opal, which fuses three complementary diagnostic sources: Roofline analysis says whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound, PC stall sampling says which source lines stall and why, and hardware-counter analysis says which events correlate with slowdown. Opal keeps only the salient signals, which shrinks the PC-sampling input for one kernel by 99.9% to under 6 KB, and requires the LLM to tie every edit to the diagnostic it addresses.

Opal showed that diagnostics make LLM edits both correct and faster. However, each run was still a hand-driven loop, and speedup alone did not show whether an edit fixed the bottleneck it claimed to fix. To close this gap, we built OPTIMAS, a multi-agent pipeline that selects the kernels covering 80% of runtime, profiles them, builds the prompt, calls the LLM, compiles, and validates the output bit-for-bit against reference results. We also defined Evidence-Aligned Reasoning (EAR) metrics, which check that each edit cites diagnostic evidence and lands on the identified hot spot. OPTIMAS works with commercial models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) and a locally hosted one (Llama 3.1 70B).
impact:
Across 1,640 Opal experiments on eight GPU applications and 68 input configurations, every generated version but one passed the benchmark's correctness tests, and edits cut execution time by up to 87.6% (33.3% on average). OPTIMAS, published at KDD 2026 (18.5% acceptance rate), generated correct code in all 3,410 experiments and improved performance in more than 98.82% of them, with average gains of 8.02% to 79.09% on NVIDIA GPUs.

One optimization iteration takes under 10 minutes, while collecting profiles for SW4Lite took 16 to 24 hours, and the full set of GPT-5 experiments cost $9.83 in API fees. We released every prompt, LLM response, and runtime measurement as an open dataset. Supported by an AMD academic gift, we are integrating Opal into AMD's ROCm software stack.

problem: HPC users must choose node counts, GPU counts, task binding, and power settings, and each choice moves runtime, energy, and variability in different directions. Users ask three questions over and over: what configuration to start with, how to change a run that missed its goal, and what will happen if one parameter changes. Facility operators face the same trade-offs at system scale.
importance: A single misconfigured parameter can introduce 4x run-to-run variation, so performance is a trade-off space, not a single target. Users who guess wrong either request too few nodes and risk termination, or too many and waste energy and allocation. Facilities cannot test a new scheduling policy on a production machine without interrupting service.
challenges: Each existing method solves one piece: autotuners return one configuration for one objective, generative models synthesize plausible configurations but cannot minimally edit a prior run, counterfactual methods such as DiCE edit a run but do not check domain rules, and predictive models estimate outcomes but cannot generate alternatives. Without constraint checking, a model can return a configuration that looks valid but cannot run, such as 16 GPUs on fewer than 4 nodes of Marconi100, which has 4 GPUs per node. Production telemetry adds missing entries, inconsistent counters, and traces of billions of rows.
approach:
We started with system-level decisions. With collaborators at ORNL, NREL, LLNL, and Colorado State, we extended the ExaDigiT digital twin with scheduling (S-RAPS), so facilities can evaluate scheduling policies and incentive structures against simulated power and cooling before deployment. To choose node counts under runtime-power trade-offs, we paired attention-based embeddings of job telemetry with multi-objective Bayesian optimization and active sample acquisition.

However, while schedulers became smarter, computational scientists were left without tools to navigate design spaces with hundreds of parameters. To bridge this gap, we built WANDER, a query-driven system that unifies prediction, counterfactual generation, and recommendation behind one interface and scores each suggestion by prediction uncertainty, agreement with a causal model, and similarity to historical data. COMPASS then formalizes the three user questions as recommend, reconfigure, and what-if queries and solves all three with one loss, Conditional Constrained Counterfactual Generation, which encodes validity, closeness to the user's baseline, user constraints, and diversity. Each suggestion is labeled trusted, caution, or unsupported, lists the observed samples behind it, and, when no data supports a region, names configurations to run next.
impact:
Integrated with a validated scheduler simulator on production traces, COMPASS cut average job turnaround time by 25.53% and allocated 67.77% fewer nodes than ModelX, a state-of-the-art ML-based scheduler; against the user-specified baseline, the reductions are 65.93% and 80.93%. On real hardware, configurations COMPASS labels trusted ran within 13.31% of their predicted execution times, and it scaled to a 1.3-billion-sample, 126 GB trace with up to 80x faster inference than the GReaT generative baseline.

On the Adastra production dataset, attention-based embeddings improved Pareto hypervolume by 37% over direct regression, and active sampling cut end-to-end time by 27% while using 50 to 75% of the data. In the S-RAPS digital twin, which loads public traces from Frontier, Marconi100, Fugaku, Lassen, and Adastra, an ML-guided policy gave the lowest turnaround time and energy-delay product under high load on Fugaku.

problem: New architectures arrive about every six months, and users, schedulers, and procurement teams must decide which platform to use before anyone has measured their applications on it. A performance model for each new system and application takes days or weeks of data collection. We want to predict performance on a new machine from a handful of runs.
importance: A prediction that needs only a few target runs turns a weeks-long measurement campaign into a short pilot, and lets a scheduler place jobs on machines it has barely observed. It also lets procurement teams compare candidate systems using the measurements they already have.
challenges: Unlike images or text, where samples share a fixed geometry of pixels or words, HPC telemetry has incompatible feature spaces: L3-cache counters on Intel systems do not exist on IBM BG/Q, and NVIDIA counters share nothing with AMD ones. Standard transfer learning, such as fine-tuning and linear probing, assumes source and target share the same features, so it cannot adapt a model across architectures, and a few samples are too few to train from scratch. Static machine descriptions such as core counts miss dynamic behavior such as achievable memory bandwidth.
approach:
We cast the task as relative performance: the ratio of an application's runtime on a target machine to its runtime on a reference machine, which removes effects such as iteration count. We first studied semi-supervised learning for this task, then found that few-shot learning is the key: few-shot adaptation, multi-source models, and LLM-generated samples each improved cross-platform transfer.

However, few-shot adaptation still assumes the two datasets share features. To remove that assumption, we built ModelX, a test-time adaptation method that learns an input alignment mapping target features into the source model's space, and, if unaligned features remain, stacks a residual network trained on the few target samples; a severity measure tells us when alignment alone is enough. ModelXc then extends ModelX from regression to classification and uses it to personalize fall detection for older adults from a few labeled samples per person. Robust transfer also requires describing the machines themselves, so we introduced the Abstract Machine Model (AMM) in xAMM: an attention-based embedding, built from RAJAPerf runs, that encodes a machine's bandwidth, compute intensity, and scaling behavior as one vector.
impact:
ModelX outperformed fine-tuning, linear probing, and few-shot retraining across 11 HPC and 4 ML datasets, and matched a fully supervised model trained on up to 100x more target data while using only 1 to 5% of the target samples. For OpenMC, 4 new samples were enough to predict performance from Intel Sandy Bridge to IBM BG/Q and back. Used to pick job configurations on real job traces, ModelX cut average turnaround time by 71% and the resources needed for the same turnaround by 42%.

xAMM reduced XGBoost's prediction error (MAPE) by 49.64% for CPU-to-CPU and 99.07% for CPU-to-GPU prediction across LLNL's Quartz, Ruby, and Corona.

problem: Representing large amounts of heterogeneous performance data is the first step toward using machine learning for performance modeling. HPC data comes as source code, as tables with one row per run, and as streams of function executions from monitoring systems. Standard flat neural networks learn only feature-to-feature relationships inside each sample, so they miss the structure that separates a symptom from a root cause.
importance: Schedulers use runtime estimates as a hard cutoff: a job that runs past its estimate is evicted, and an overestimate leaves nodes idle. Anomalies caused by contention or hardware problems waste allocation until someone finds them. Developers learn about performance only after they run their code. Better representations improve all three predictions without the feature engineering that today needs a human in the loop.
challenges: Graph neural networks work well when a graph already exists, as in social networks, but a performance dataset has no graph; one must be built, and the choice of edges decides what the model can learn. Performance tables have missing counter values and arrive as streams, which breaks models such as XGBoost and TabNet. Source code carries its structure in a tree, but runtime also depends on the machine, the input, and the OS, none of which appear in the code. Every one of these models needs many samples, and each sample means running the application again.
approach:
We began with code. To predict whether a code change makes a program faster, we compare two correct solutions to the same problem, so machine and input effects cancel and only structure remains; a tree-based LSTM reads each solution's abstract syntax tree, trained on a corpus we built of 4,313,322 correct C++ solutions to 1,278 Codeforces problems. We later extended this into structure-aware representations for performance prediction.

We then carried the idea of structure to tabular data with Performance-in-a-Graph (PinG): each run becomes a node linked to its most similar runs, and a self-supervised GNN refines the edges and learns an embedding per run, so a new run can join the graph without rebuilding it. With Brookhaven National Laboratory, we applied the same idea to anomalies in the Chimbuko monitoring system, turning each execution event into a node and anomaly detection into node classification. However, a real-time monitor cannot afford a deep model on every event, so we designed a lightweight signal-processing detector that treats anomalies as noise and finds them with FFT, and a visual tool that lets users explore anomaly provenance databases.

Finally, because every model needs data, we built PerfGen to synthesize performance samples with generative AI and to score them with Dissimilarity, a metric that tracks downstream accuracy. Because LLMs struggle with the semantics of systems data, we designed context-enriched prompts that describe each feature.
impact:
The code models predicted whether a solution is faster or slower up to 84% of the time when trained on a single problem and 73% on 100 problems, against 68.5% for the best graph convolutional network, and the 4.3-million-solution corpus is released. Across ten HPC datasets and with up to 25% of values missing, PinG cut MSE by up to 61.67% on HPC data and 78.56% on ML data over a DNN baseline.

On Chimbuko traces from the Grid lattice-QCD code, a graph model classified anomalies with 95% accuracy against 80% for XGBoost, and graph-based classification beat gradient-based methods in 6 of 11 experiments. The FFT detector improved accuracy x F1 per unit overhead by up to 99% on benchmarks and 93% on Chimbuko traces, and the visual tool explores provenance databases with 200K to more than 16M anomaly entries in seconds. With enriched prompts, LLM-generated data reached baseline quality in under a quarter of the training epochs.

problem: Before an application can be optimized or autotuned, someone has to find out how it interacts with the hardware: which caches, memory paths, and stalls drive its execution time. The HPC ecosystem is full of isolated measurement utilities, but they do not explain behavior. Vendor profilers are often opaque, a modern GPU exposes hundreds of counters, and interfaces such as PAPI set a high bar for non-experts.
importance: Characterization is the prerequisite to every optimization: without it, tuning treats symptoms. Developers and autotuners usually judge an optimization only by execution time, so they do not see whether it leaves the GPU's streaming multiprocessors idle, and autotuners such as GPTune recommend parameter values without saying why they work. Users therefore cannot learn which bottleneck a setting removed or carry the lesson to the next code.
challenges: Collecting GPU counters is itself hard: NVIDIA's CUPTI instruments every kernel in a module, so overhead grows with the number of kernels, and no utility listed which events can be collected together, so users grouped counters by hand. Profilers report raw, timestamped counts without saying which resource matters statistically for a target metric. Dimensionality reduction hides which hardware resource a result refers to, and counter names differ across tools and systems, which rules out a fixed mapping from counters to resources.
approach:
We use existing tools when they suffice and build new instrumentation when they do not. LIBNVCD measures application-hardware interactions on NVIDIA GPUs with three function calls in the source, lets users pick which kernels to profile, and finds on its own which events can be measured together.

On top of this data layer, we built DASHING, a programmable analysis and visualization framework that groups counters by hardware resource and uses sparse-coding regression to score each resource by how well it predicts a target metric, with a web dashboard for exploring large hierarchical data. We then designed a composite target that combines execution time and SM utilization, characterized six common GPU optimizations with it, and turned the resource-usage patterns into optimization suggestions for ECP proxy applications. To reach autotuner users, we integrated DASHING into LBNL's GPTune. As AI became a major HPC workload, we applied the same characterization to deep learning optimizers training recurrent networks on AMD MI100 GPUs.
impact:
LIBNVCD adds a mean overhead below 1% over raw CUPTI and sets up 500x faster and cleans up 13x faster than hand-written CUPTI code. DASHING helped identify and fix problematic resource usage in three Exascale Computing Project applications. On Pennant's Main3 kernel, optimizations chosen from the resource analysis improved execution time by up to 29.6% and SM utilization by up to 5.4%.

In GPTune, the analysis of 410 Hypre runs on 32 Cori Haswell nodes showed which grid-size parameters track runtime and which do not. On MI100 GPUs, it identified non-uniform memory access as the most frequent issue across the deep learning optimizers. These capabilities are now being integrated into AMD's ROCm software stack.

problem: The same job, run twice with the same configuration on the same system, can take different amounts of time. On shared HPC systems this variation comes from network contention, power caps, task placement, and interference from other jobs, and in task-based workflows also from the scheduler changing task order. Users do not know which settings drive it, and the data needed to explain a slow run afterwards is rarely kept.
importance: Variation makes 'fastest configuration' a moving target: the setting with the lowest average time can also have the widest spread, so users cannot plan allocations or compare results. Workflows that combine simulation, analytics, and AI on DOE leadership systems add more layers where variation enters. Reproducible performance needs both an understanding of the causes and data that others can find and reuse.
challenges: Earlier studies looked at one source of variation at a time and found influential parameters by sweeping the whole space, which does not scale: five knobs on one cluster already give 540 combinations. The tools that record performance data, such as Darshan for I/O, Chimbuko for trace anomalies, and RADICAL-Cybertools for task execution, were not designed to work together, and metadata is usually added after the run, piece by piece. At the GPU level, a single trace reaches hundreds of gigabytes per run, and existing tools read it sequentially on one node.
approach:
We first measured what causes variation. On a 324-node production cluster at LLNL, we varied node count, cores per node, network bandwidth level, power cap, and rank placement for five benchmarks under an interfering job, and ranked parameters with a desirability score that rewards low average time and low variation and an influence score based on graph signal analysis.

However, explaining variation in a workflow requires data that current practice does not keep. To close this gap, we co-led the ASCR-funded RECUP project with Brookhaven, Sandia, and Argonne National Laboratories to build a FAIR performance data framework. We mapped the challenges of FAIR digital objects in HPC workflows and proposals for FAIR, automated workflows, then designed a pipeline that combines RADICAL-Cybertools, Darshan, Chimbuko, Mochi, and DataStates and stores metadata as RO-Crate. For Dask workflows, we stream task provenance through Mochi and record thread-level I/O with Darshan in one table, and we studied performance analysis and data reduction for exascale workflows. We also helped shape community practice on reproducibility across HPC and distributed environments.

To find causes inside GPU traces, we split Nsight traces into time shards that MPI ranks analyze in parallel and fit causal graphs linking kernel and memory features to run-to-run variation. Because I/O is itself a source of slowdown, we carried McrEngine's aggregation methods into workflows: first for small-file writes in bioinformatics pipelines, then in FILCIO, which intercepts C stdio calls and gathers small writes in memory before they reach disk, with no change to the application.
impact:
On the 324-node cluster, network bandwidth level most affected repeatability, and the analysis cut the configurations a user must evaluate for a new strong-scaling application by up to 97%; the finding held two years later after system and software upgrades. In a Dask XGBoost workflow on Polaris, the combined provenance and I/O data linked long-running, I/O-fused tasks to 297 unresponsive event-loop warnings in the first 500 seconds, a blind spot in the interaction between workflows and the orchestration layer.

The distributed GPU-trace analysis ran 67% faster at 1,024 MPI ranks than at 128 on four traces of about 93 million samples each, and showed that larger grid dimensions and device-to-device copies go with more kernel variability. FILCIO gave a 1.75x speedup on a program that spends nearly all its runtime writing to disk.

problem: HPC schedulers must decide where each job runs across heterogeneous CPUs and GPUs. The same decision now sits inside a single edge node, which combines a CPU with an integrated GPU and must run streaming deep learning inference within deadlines. Using one device at a time, or splitting jobs evenly, leaves capacity unused because each device runs the same model at a different speed.
importance: Most research scales inference across distributed edge clouds and leaves the heterogeneous resources inside each node underused. Using them well gives more inference throughput from hardware that is already deployed. Device speed also drifts with temperature and power management, so a schedule that meets deadlines now can miss them later.
challenges: On-node scheduling had received less attention than cross-node scaling, so no scheduler divided a streaming inference workload across a node's CPU and integrated GPU under deadlines. Assigning jobs to devices with different speeds is combinatorial, and heuristics such as genetic algorithms or task partitioning do not guarantee the best assignment. Adaptive schedulers recompute mappings online with heuristic search or learning, and that overhead grows with the workload.
approach:
We first introduced a heterogeneous hyperperiod, based on the cyclic executive used in real-time systems: each device gets the same time in every window, and jobs are scheduled inside those windows. However, the heuristic assignment inside each window gave no optimality guarantee, so we formulated rate monotonic scheduling across heterogeneous devices as an integer linear program that finds optimal assignments for streaming applications with deadlines.

An optimal schedule is still expensive to recompute when device speed drifts. To remove that cost, we separated optimization from operation: we discretize each device's health using normalized frequency, power, and utilization, build a table of schedulable assignments offline for every health combination, and at runtime switch tables in constant time.
impact: The hyperperiod scheduler improved AlexNet and GoogLeNet-v1 image-classification performance by 1.5% to 48.1% over single-device and even-split baselines. The ILP-based rate monotonic scheduler improved inference efficiency by up to 5.26% over genetic-algorithm and task-partition scheduling and received the Best Paper Award at IEEE Cloud Summit 2025. The offline, health-indexed scheduler cut runtime scheduling overhead by about 28x compared with heuristic-search and learning-based adaptive schedulers.

problem: Because performance data behaves like scientific data, the methods we build for it apply well beyond HPC. Learning from few labeled samples, reconstructing a large space from a small sample, and generating parallel code are the same problems in health care, structural biology, and scientific simulation. In each case, labeled data is scarce or the space of possibilities is too large to measure.
importance: Autistic college students have a higher dropout rate than neurotypical students, and physiological distress, depression, and anxiety are among the main causes; predicting stress onset could support real-time intervention. A fall-detection model that works on average can still miss how one person moves. In structural biology, wet-lab mutation experiments can take months for even a small set of mutants, and the effect of two mutations cannot be predicted by adding the effects of each one alone.
challenges: Physiological data from wearables comes with few reliable stress labels, and autistic and neurotypical students may respond differently. Personalizing a model runs into the same obstacle our transfer-learning work addresses in HPC: each person provides too few samples to train from scratch. For proteins, the number of mutants grows combinatorially: a 99-residue protein has 1,751,211 unique mutants with two substitutions, so even fast computational screening becomes intractable.
approach:
We adapted our analytics frameworks to clinical health data. In a mixed-method study with 20 college students (10 autistic, 10 neurotypical), we combined unsupervised representation learning with semi-supervised label approximation to predict stress onset from mobile and wearable data. Our few-shot transfer-learning methods apply here as well: for example, ModelXc extends ModelX, our transfer-learning method for datasets with mismatched features, to personalize fall detection for older adults from a few samples per person (see Few-Shot Transfer Learning for Performance).

In structural biology, we generated every mutant with two amino-acid substitutions for 8 proteins, scored each with rigidity analysis, and rebuilt the full impact map from a small sample under a low-rank constraint that smooths sampling noise; a later book chapter extended these low-rank methods. In scientific simulation, ACAC generates parallel MPI+OpenMP, MPI+CUDA, and MPI+HIP code for cellular automata, which model material diffusion and the spread of fire or disease, with no programming effort from users. Earlier, Eunomia protected wireless medical devices from interference by switching channels proactively and letting low-priority devices defer to safety-critical ones.
impact: The stress models predicted stress onset with 69% accuracy for autistic students, 72% for neurotypical students, and 70% for both groups together. The mutation work showed that the effect of two substitutions can be approximated from as few as 25% of all mutants, and the low-rank constraint cut reconstruction error by up to 34% for one protein. For a cellular automaton with 2.36M cells, ACAC's generated code ran up to 544.2x faster than a sequential baseline on GPUs and up to 16.8x faster than a specialized FPGA implementation, and it scales simulations to 10 billion cells.

problem: A large system is only as usable as the software between the scientist and the hardware. Every layer of that stack can become the bottleneck: the network on a chip, the numerical precision of a program, the storage that holds its files, and the gateway through which a researcher reaches the machine. Each layer needs its own tool.
importance: Hardware designers must evaluate on-chip networks before the chip exists. Numerical precision decides both a program's accuracy and how fast it runs. Distributed burst buffers give storage bandwidth that grows with node count, but only if metadata keeps up. The Network for Earthquake Engineering Simulation (NEES) connected 14 labs whose researchers needed XSEDE, the Open Science Grid, and Purdue supercomputers without learning each one's interface.
challenges: In burst buffers, metadata for files shared across many processes must live in a global index that thousands of processes access at once, so metadata management, not bandwidth, limits scalability. Deciding by hand which variables can use lower precision without hurting accuracy does not scale to large codes. Each computing venue has its own submission interface, and researchers would otherwise have to learn all of them.
approach: We built tools at each of these layers. At the chip, GpNoCSim is a general-purpose simulator for networks-on-chip, which we later extended. In the program, we built a tool that automatically generates mixed-precision versions of a code. In storage, MetaKV adds metadata services to an existing key-value store for the bursty, concurrent workloads of distributed burst buffers: compressed storage management, supervised block clustering, and log-ring based collective message reduction. At the facility, BatchSubmit lets NEES researchers run on XSEDE, the Open Science Grid, Purdue supercomputers, and NEEShub servers through the NEEShub science gateway.
impact: MetaKV sped up metadata put and get operations by up to 2.66x and 6.29x over state-of-the-art key-value stores, and its benefit grows with metadata load. Through BatchSubmit, researchers across the 14 NEES labs submit simulations to XSEDE, the Open Science Grid, and Purdue supercomputers from one science gateway instead of learning each venue's interface.

problem: Recent workforce efforts prepare students to write programs for heterogeneous HPC platforms, but computation is only one of the three tasks an HPC application performs; the other two are communication and I/O. At the same time, AI is changing how scientific software is built and who builds it, and the training pipelines behind scientific computing must change with it.
importance: Network bandwidth is not scaling with compute, so moving the data these applications generate slows scientific progress. Scaling data-intensive applications is a problem shared by high-performance, high-throughput, and cloud computing, so training in it reaches far. No single university can set training and collaboration practice for the whole scientific computing ecosystem.
challenges: A data-driven analysis of existing curricula shows that most do not prepare students to consider the design choices that scale parallel I/O. Teaching it requires hands-on access to systems where I/O actually becomes the bottleneck, not only programming exercises.
approach: We designed HPC@SCALE, a hands-on course at Texas State University that trains students to build scalable end-to-end system software with a focus on minimizing parallel I/O. Beyond the classroom, we take part in the Next-Generation Ecosystems for Scientific Computing (NGE) workshop series, a three-year effort to build scientific computing ecosystems through socio-technical co-design: the intentional integration of social and technical components as parts of one strategy. We are also bringing our Opal optimization framework into the curriculum, so students learn performance engineering with the tools we build.
impact: HPC@SCALE was presented as an invited paper at the EduHiPC workshop at HiPC 2021. The 2025 NGE workshop convened more than 40 experts from national laboratories, academia, industry, and community organizations, and its report recommends modular, trustworthy AI-enabled scientific software and training pipelines that keep pace with technological change. The 2026 report turns four strategic themes, including workforce, pedagogy, and governance, into eight priorities for community action.

problem: Production science codes are often too large, too complex to set up, or too restricted to distribute for early hardware design studies, so co-design teams use proxy applications: compact codes that extract one performance-critical kernel. XSBench, for example, extracts the cross-section lookup that accounts for about 85% of OpenMC's runtime. A proxy is only useful if it stresses the hardware the way its parent does.
importance: Architects and procurement teams make multi-million-dollar decisions from proxy measurements. If a proxy misses a resource bottleneck that limits its parent, those decisions rest on the wrong behavior, and developers optimize a code that does not represent the target workload.
challenges: Prior approaches equated similarity between applications with matching their runtime and did not account for how each application interacts with the hardware. Earlier validation, including our own XSBench study, correlated hardware counters with efficiency loss one at a time, which cannot find groups of counters that together explain performance. PCA and CCA handle groups but mix counters into features that no longer name a resource, and counters differ by architecture.
approach:
We began by co-developing XSBench with Argonne's CESAR team and verifying it against OpenMC using 47 hardware counters on Intel Xeon. That study showed the limit of one-counter-at-a-time validation, so we led a multi-laboratory effort to define what similarity should mean for proxy applications and how to validate it across architectures.

The resulting method, VERITAS, asks two questions for each hardware resource: how much the resource predicts the parent's loss of parallel efficiency, and how well the proxy reproduces the parent's use of it. It fits a sparse model of efficiency loss over all counters and adds up the weight of each resource group into a Resource Significance Measure, then compares low-dimensional subspaces of each application's counters to give a Coverage score between 0 and 1. Because both scores are per resource, they compare the same resources across architectures while still naming the counters behind them. We then applied the method to CMT-Bone, the proxy for the CMT-nek multiphase-flow code, and PADDLE later automated the coverage workflow inside a general machine-learning environment for performance data.
impact: XSBench's scaling efficiency and floating-point rate fall within 5% of OpenMC's, and the DOE Exascale Computing Project adopted it as the standard proxy for OpenMC. VERITAS showed that XSBench covers 80% of OpenMC's memory behavior on Xeon and 90% of its L2 behavior on Blue Gene/Q, while RSBench, which cuts memory use from 5.6 GB to 41 MB by recomputing data, covers only about 75%. Applying the method, we found that the CMT-Bone proxy developed by the NNSA PSAAP II center did not match its parent's behavior and guided its remediation. PADDLE reproduced the published XSBench coverage result through its automated pipeline.

problem: MPI is how most HPC applications communicate, yet two parts of its behavior were out of reach. Tools could see calls between the application and the MPI library, but not what happens inside the library. And when a process failed, the MPI standard left the library's state undefined, so most applications could do little more than abort.
importance: Internal library behavior, such as which receive queue matches a message or how a protocol is configured, decides communication performance, yet it was invisible without implementation-specific hacks. Process failures usually terminate the whole application, so large runs lose all the work since their last checkpoint. Both gaps grow with scale.
challenges: MPI 3.0 added the MPI_T interface to expose internal performance and control variables, but because an earlier interface, PERUSE, failed standardization by defining events that did not match every implementation, MPI_T defines no variables at all; each library decides what to expose, so tools must discover variables at run time. For fault tolerance, the ULFM proposal supplies failure detection and repair, but using it requires large code changes, error handlers do not tell the programmer where a failure happened, and FA-MPI works only for non-blocking operations.
approach:
To expose internal MPI dynamics, we wrote a user's introduction to MPI_T and built the first tools on it. Varlist queries and lists every variable a library exposes, so a job script can record the exact MPI configuration of a run, and Gyan is a lightweight profiler that reads performance variables at the start and end of a run and reports their sum, minimum, and maximum across ranks. We applied both to the NAS BT benchmark and to NEK5000 on Open MPI and MVAPICH2, and extended the study in a journal version.

For resilience, we helped design the Fault Tolerance Assistant (FTA), a try/catch programming model for MPI. Programmers wrap MPI calls in a TRY block; at the end of the block all ranks agree on whether a failure occurred, which localizes it to that block, and FTA repairs every communicator automatically before a RETRY restarts the block.
impact: Monitoring all MPI_T performance variables with Gyan changed average run time by less than 0.5%, below the noise threshold. On BT, Gyan showed that larger problems push more messages through the unexpected receive queue, which points to specific receives to reschedule; on NEK5000, it showed that MVAPICH2's blocking mode raises run time by 28% at 64 processes. We demonstrated FTA's shrinking and non-shrinking recovery on a synthetic code and on the CoMD molecular dynamics proxy application.

problem: Because failures are routine at scale, HPC systems rely on checkpoint/restart, which periodically saves application state so a failed job can resume. Checkpointing accounts for 75 to 80% of the I/O traffic on HPC systems, and I/O bandwidth is not keeping pace with compute, so resilience itself has become a limiter of scalability. Power limits add a second cost: a job capped at a fixed per-node power bound slows down during computation even though it leaves power unused while it writes I/O.
importance: When checkpoints are expensive, applications checkpoint less often, and each failure throws away more computation. On a power-limited system, power left idle during one job's I/O phase is performance another job could have used. Both costs grow with machine size.
challenges: On shared grids, spare disks on the grid's own machines can replace distant checkpoint servers, but those hosts leave, get loaded by their owners, or fail, and earlier failure models covered compute hosts, not storage hosts. On supercomputers, general-purpose compressors gain little on scientific data, and merging checkpoints in rank order does not place similar data together. Lossy compression shrinks checkpoints further, but no one knew whether a restart from an inexact state still gives a correct answer. For power, earlier work shifted power only among the nodes of one job.
approach:
We reduced the cost of resilience with two complementary methods, intelligent storage placement and intelligent compression, and built each into a framework for a different setting. For volatile cycle-sharing grids, FALCON stores checkpoints on the grid's own machines: it models each storage host with multiple failure states, weighs failure probability, CPU load, and network bandwidth to pick stable hosts, and splits each checkpoint into erasure-coded fragments.

For bandwidth-limited supercomputers, McrEngine reads the metadata in HDF5 and netCDF checkpoints, groups variables with the same name and type across processes, and compresses each group with the algorithm that suits it, while aggregating on a few nodes cuts the number of concurrent writers. We then tested how far compression can go by checkpointing the ChaNGa cosmology code with lossy compression and checking the physical output after injected failures. This work formed the basis of our dissertation.

Because I/O phases, including checkpoints, draw less power than computation, we then designed algorithms that move power from jobs in I/O phases to jobs computing, including a scheduler that staggers jobs so fewer do I/O at once.
impact: On Purdue's production Condor pool of 20,000 processors, FALCON improved application performance by 11% to 44% over Condor's own checkpointing, and it was deployed on Purdue's campus grid. McrEngine improved compression by up to 115% over concatenate-and-compress, cut checkpoint overhead by up to 87% and restart overhead by up to 62%, and its methods are now integrated into the Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR) library, which won an R&D 100 award and supports LLNL's El Capitan exascale system. Lossy compression shrank ChaNGa checkpoints to 15% of their original size while giving correct results after 3 to 70 injected failures. I/O-aware power shifting improved average performance by up to 8% and a high-priority job by up to 32%.
